latest.title: Sport-Concussion Identification and Attitudes and the Role of the Mass Media Broadcaster: Does it Matter What We See and Hear?
latest.abstract: Professional commentary in live sport broadcasts can mischaracterize concussion, potentially undermining audiences’ understanding and opinions about this commentary. An online experimental survey (N = 163) was conducted where participants saw footage of a suspected concussion with either no commentary, or high-, or low-quality commentary from a health perspective. No commentary effect was found for concussion identification or attitudes; however, there were ceiling effects on both measures, and secondary analyses revealed that the footage, and not the commentary, was most memorable to participants. Further studies are needed to determine if live broadcast commentary does play a role in public understanding of sport-concussion.

latest.title: Fun Facts: The Impact of Joke Proximity on Encoding Facts from the Main Stories on Last Week Tonight with John Oliver
latest.abstract: Drawing from Dynamic Human Centered Communication Systems Theory (DHCCST), this study examines how humor influences the acquisition of factual information from comedic news, using an experimental design with a recognition task and a psychophysiological measure. Participants paid greater attention, indicated by heart rate deceleration, to facts that followed the presentation of a joke in the main stories on Last Week Tonight with John Oliver. Humor enhanced recognition of facts presented in close proximity both before and after jokes, indicating better encoding of facts, particularly when the facts and proximal jokes were related.

latest.title: Tolerating Toxicity: How Incivility and Belief Congruence in User-Generated Comments Affect Readers’ Motivational Activation and Information Intake
latest.abstract: By conceptualizing incivility and belief congruence in online comments as message features that elicit motivational system activation, this study investigates how these features influence readers’ real-time psychophysiological responses, self-reported emotional responses, memory, and behavioral intention. The findings revealed that uncivil comments did not elicit stronger physiological responses (i.e. skin conductance and corrugator activity) than civil ones, suggesting that social media users may not be highly reactive to incivility in online news comments. In contrast, belief-incongruent comments triggered increased anger and behavioral approach tendencies. Further, for belief-congruent comments, memory encoding was more accurate and sensitive for uncivil comments than civil ones.

latest.title: Contagious Smiles on Screen. The Role of Emotional Alignment of TV Presenters
latest.abstract: Despite extensive research on smiling, gaps remain in understanding its dynamic impact on audience responses to televised presenters. Grounded in Emotional Contagion Theory, this study investigates how a presenter’s smile influences viewer engagement, emotional mimicry, and evaluations of credibility and effectiveness. Using a controlled laboratory experiment employing a factorial within–between design, 120 participants watched video clips of TV presenters delivering identical messages either with or without smiling. Physiological arousal (electrodermal activity), attention (heart rate), emotional mimicry (via facial recognition), and self-reported perceptions were recorded. Smiling presenters elicited significantly higher arousal, greater mimicry, enhanced attention, and more favorable evaluations compared to neutral-faced presenters. Additionally, negative emotions such as disgust and contempt emerged in response to non-smiling presenters, supporting the broader applicability of emotional contagion. Gender differences showed that female viewers displayed stronger mimicry and rated smiling presenters more positively. The study offers novel insights into nonverbal communication in media contexts and underscores the strategic value of facial expressions for enhancing the perceived credibility and effectiveness of on-screen communicators.

latest.title: Tracking the Roots of Low News Usage on Smartphones – Do Individual Interests, Political Attitudes, and Media Consumption Habits Affect the Mobile News Use of Young Adults?
latest.abstract: While democratic opinion formation relies on citizens receiving vital information from the news, an increasing number of people consistently consume very little of it. To address this concern, we tracked the mobile news consumption of 382 young adults in Switzerland and combined it with survey data of the participants to determine the effect of topical interests, political attitudes, and media consumption habits on news usage. We found that interest in domestic politics was a strong predictor of news consumption. Additional predictors within our 18–25-year-old participant group were age and time spent online. These findings have implications for policymakers; fostering an informed citizenry may be more effective when targeting the underlying interest in politics rather than directly attempting to boost news use.

latest.title: Media Exposure Diversity: An Empirical Explication
latest.abstract: This paper explicates the concept of media exposure diversity in the context of presidential elections. Analyzing data from the 2012, 2016, and 2020 American National Election Survey, we created two proxies of media exposure diversity: diversity in media types and diversity in ideological content. Findings show that levels of exposure diversity were moderate and relatively stable; higher exposure diversity levels suggest active choices, as the two indices correlated positively with education, political interest, and levels of news exposure. Moreover, revealing the potential positive roles of exposure diversity, the two indices were positively related to democratic citizenship outcomes beyond stringent controls.

latest.title: How Parental Mediation Affects Adolescent Short-Form Video Addiction: Variable-Centered and Person-Centered Perspectives
latest.abstract: Grounded in ecological techno-subsystem theory, this study examined the impact of parental mediation on adolescent short-form video addiction (SFVA), and the mediating role of the parent-child relationship. A survey was conducted among 1326 Chinese middle school students. The variable-centered analyses revealed that the parent-child relationship mediated the influence of parental supervision, modeling, and involvement on SFVA. Person-centered analyses identified six distinct parental mediation profiles; compared to the control-oriented profile, all others significantly influenced SFVA via the parent-child relationship. These findings provide valuable insights into a more comprehensive understanding of the multifaceted impacts and mechanisms of parental mediation on SFVA.

latest.title: PolitiTalk: Analyzing the Relationship Between Partisan Podcast Use and Political Participation
latest.abstract: As podcasts become more prevalent in contemporary American media diets, it is important to more deeply examine their role as a source of political news and information. The current research examines the relationship between political podcast usage among adults in the United States and political participation. Survey results suggest a correlation between political podcast use and high-effort and low-effort forms of political participation. Specifically, use of liberal podcasts was associated with higher levels of political participation among all participants, but use of conservative podcasts was only associated with low-effort activities. The findings speak to the significance podcasts play in the partisan media landscape and the asymmetry of partisan media in the country.

trending.title: How Autonomy of Artificial Intelligence Technology and User Agency Influence AI Perceptions and Attitudes: Applying the Theory of Psychological Reactance
trending.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technology is increasingly taking over various aspects of our daily decision-making processes. The current study investigates how media users emotionally and cognitively respond to the increasing autonomy of AI technology. A survey (N = 297) measured the perceived autonomy of AI applications that individuals currently use and examined its relationship with psychological reactance, user agency, and perceived personalization. Findings show that AI autonomy is positively related to threat to freedom and psychological reactance. However, AI autonomy is also positively associated with personalization, which cancels out the negative impact of psychological reactance on attitudes. Those who feel a higher agency perceive a higher threat to freedom as perceived AI autonomy increases. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

trending.title: The Role of User Empowerment, AI Hallucination, and Privacy Concerns in Continued Use and Premium Subscription Intentions: An Extended Technology Acceptance Model for Generative AI
trending.abstract: This study extends the Technology Acceptance Model for Generative AI (GAI) by incorporating perceived user empowerment (PUE) and two risk factors – privacy concerns and hallucination risks. A survey of 783 U.S. GAI users revealed that PUE directly influenced continuance intention (CI) and willingness to pay for premium service (PAY) and indirectly affected CI through attitude toward AI (ATTAI). Perceived ease of use was indirectly linked to CI via ATTAI. Privacy concerns negatively affected CI, while hallucination risks negatively influenced ATTAI, which reduced CI. The findings underscore the role of PUE and risk perceptions in CI and PAY for GAI.

trending.title: Social Media News Use Amplifies the Illusory Truth Effects of Viral Deepfakes: A Cross-National Study of Eight Countries
trending.abstract: This study enhances our understanding of illusory truth effects (ITE) by focusing on deepfakes. Survey data from eight countries demonstrates ITE – such that those exposed to deepfakes previously were more likely to perceive the misinformation as accurate than those exposed to them for the first time. This pattern was observed regardless of the political and nonpolitical nature of deepfakes across all sociopolitical settings. Also, those who rely on social media for news are found to be more susceptible to deepfakes. Moreover, relying on social media for news consumption amplified ITE for all individuals (regardless of cognitive ability levels).

trending.title: ‘Zero Human Emotion’: AI Anchors and the Normative Repercussions
trending.abstract: This study utilizes thematic analysis to analyze content disseminated by Artificial Intelligence (AI) anchors. Researchers analyzed content from a private TV channel from Pakistan. The channel produces a news program that delivers content to viewers, but said content is delivered through broadcast anchors generated by AI. The findings are analyzed through the lens of the hierarchy of influences, which allows researchers to understand influences on content from multiple levels of analyses. The study not only illustrates why AI anchors pose a threat to journalism’s normative notions undergirding the field, but also how utilizing AI anchors opens avenues to non-journalistic actors to have increasing influence over news production.

trending.title: Silencing Online Incivility: Examining the Effects of Impoliteness and Intolerance in Online Political Discussions
trending.abstract: Drawing on silencing and online incivility literature, this study examined how people evaluate and respond to impolite and intolerant online opinions in different discussion contexts. Based on a between-subject online survey experiment in the U.S. (N = 959), we found that people perceived impoliteness and intolerance as uncivil, leading to intentions to silence others. The results also revealed that intolerance resulted in higher perceived incivility and silencing intentions compared to impoliteness. Furthermore, the direct effects of impoliteness and intolerance on perceived incivility and their indirect effects on silencing intentions through perceived incivility were stronger in agreeing discussions than in disagreeing ones. However, social endorsement cues did not moderate the mechanisms.

trending.title: From Podcasts to Protests: Examining the Influence of Podcasts and Misinformation on Contentious Political Participation
trending.abstract: As distrust in mainstream media rises, audiences increasingly turn toward alternative news sources. This study examines the impact of alternative non-mainstream podcast news use on contentious political participation through misinformation belief and sharing. Findings from a sample of US adults (N = 797) indicate that alternative non-mainstream podcast news use is significantly associated with misinformation belief and sharing. In addition, alternative non-mainstream podcast news use is related to an increase in contentious political participation through misinformation sharing only. Ultimately, we find that political identity strength moderates the relationship between alternative non-mainstream podcast news use and contentious political participation only through misinformation belief.

trending.title: Indirect Media Effects on the Adoption of Artificial Intelligence: The Roles of Perceived and Actual Knowledge in the Influence of Presumed Media Influence Model
trending.abstract: To examine the indirect media effects on the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), we employed the influence of presumed media influence (IPMI) model and its extensions. The results of an online survey of adults (N = 1,360) in Hong Kong revealed that both their media attention to AI-related information and interpersonal communication about AI influenced presumed others’ media attention. In turn, that dynamic shaped perceived descriptive norms and injunctive norms of using AI, which influenced individuals’ intention to use AI for work and/or learning. Furthermore, although persumed media influence was stronger among individuals with high perceived knowlegdge than ones with low perceived knowledge about AI, no difference emerged between individuals with high versus low actual knowlege about AI.

trending.title: Politicized and Paranoid? Assessing Attitudinal Predictors of Alternative News Consumption
trending.abstract: The study of right-wing alternative news sources has moved to the center of scholarly attention recently. Such sources cater to news consumers characterized by extreme political views and mistrust toward mainstream news. However, research into the predictors of alternative news consumption is still scarce. We approach this gap by combining online tracking and survey data from 2,009 German panel participants. We find conspiratorial thinking and pro-Russian stance to be predictors of alternative news consumption, both in absolute and in relative terms. Our analysis thus contributes to a more nuanced understanding of alternative news consumers.

trending.title: Perceived Risk and Trust in News Sources: A Multi-Group Analysis of Deepfakes and AI-Generated Misinformation
trending.abstract: This study employs the risk information seeking and processing model to examine how perceived risk, trust in news sources, and information-seeking behavior interact in the context of AI-generated misinformation and deepfakes. Using data from 300 Chinese and 263 South Korean participants, the research applies a moderated-mediation approach to assess cultural differences. Findings reveal that perceived risk reduces trust in news sources via information-seeking behavior. AI-generated misinformation amplifies this relationship, though effects vary: South Koreans engage in more information-seeking, while Chinese participants show reduced engagement, likely due to differing media environments and regulations. These insights highlight cultural nuances in misinformation response.
